title: Slow Jams: The Comics of David Choe — Cartoonist Kayfabe
summary: Jim Rugg and Ed Piskor inspect physical copies of SPX 2000, NON and the Xeric edition of Slow Jams, tracing David Choe's short comics path while reading his collage, photocopy, lettering and autobiographical techniques. The page map preserves the bicycle-revenge story, explicit masturbation spread, infatuation and violent fantasy, suicide turn, prison short, sticker-art encouragement and dated scarcity pitch while separating printed-object evidence, criticism, plot, autobiography, literal biography, rights and safety.

quality.assessment: Complete chronological human read and object-centered correction/context pass. Dense alternative-comics names, titles, grant terms and story-character damage are repaired where defensible. Unclear names and masked words remain unresolved; automatic captions contain no publisher speaker prefixes.

speaker_policy: The public hosts are Jim Rugg and Ed Piskor, but participant presence does not identify individual lines. Publish no named turns until held-out acoustic/video validation passes.

connections.relationship: SPX 2000 situates Choe among a dense alternative-comics cohort rather than treating him as an isolated celebrity artist.
Pasted text and hand lettering show the page as assembled object, not only drawing.
NON #3 and #4 connect a self-made mini-comic to a curated anthology audience.
NON #5's silkscreened package makes binding and production part of the archive evidence.
The bicycle story uses Choe's persona while the archive resists treating every plot event as literal biography.
The hosts use McCloud's transition framework to explain why Choe's image links feel less cinematic and more associative.
Waiting and a threatening note build anticipation that ends in emotional failure rather than triumph.
Destroying the recovered bicycle preserves the injury without resolving the protagonist's loss.
The hosts argue visual experiment works because autobiographical narration keeps emotional orientation.
The perfect-bound book is linked backward to a mini-comic and sideways to NON serialization.
A best-of issue functions as a pre-algorithm recommendation system for alternative comics.
Kochalka, McCloud and Young quotations show multiple critical vocabularies attaching to the debut.
Street sensibility and believable characters prompt a comparison with Jaime Hernandez rather than a claim of direct influence.
An abstinence text becomes visual material inside an explicitly sexual autobiographical book.
A released prisoner choosing a return is presented as a short fictional tragedy, not a universal claim about reentry.
The masturbation spread makes duration calculable through repeated actions and linked images.
Formal innovation does not by itself settle whether an explicit page belongs in a classroom.
A detailed face within visual chaos demonstrates how Choe controls focal hierarchy.
The annual meeting promise transforms a letter into a multi-year fantasy structure.
A wished-for reunion turns into organized humiliation and violence.
The hospital escape and suicidal turn are plot events requiring context, not isolated biographical claims.
The story moves from violent fantasy and self-destruction to a private reaffirmation rather than a clean rescue moral.
Grant evidence connects material production to a broader cohort of self-published cartoonists.
The hosts value Choe's looseness because it challenges their own fear of carrying sketchbook energy onto final pages.

source_notes.claim: The anthology is SPX 2000 and Tom Devlin edited it.
source_notes.assessment: Confirm title, editor and contributor order from the physical book/indicia; the hosts visibly handle it.

source_notes.claim: Slow Jams appeared across NON #3 and #4 after Jordan Crane saw Choe's mini-comic.
source_notes.assessment: The objects support appearance; exact discovery/meeting history needs Crane, Choe or contemporary editorial documentation.

source_notes.claim: NON #5 contains the described Choe bicycle story and Xeric-supported inserts.
source_notes.assessment: Use the physical issue's contents and colophon for exact story title, creators, date and package components.

source_notes.claim: Every event in the bicycle story happened literally to Choe.
source_notes.assessment: The hosts call the work autobiographical, but a comic protagonist and narrated event remain page evidence unless independently established.

source_notes.claim: Slow Jams was published in 1999 through a Xeric Grant after a zine edition.
source_notes.assessment: Verify year, grant cycle, publisher, print format and edition order from indicia, Xeric records and surviving copies.

source_notes.claim: The spoken Kochalka, McCloud and Young passages are exact quotations.
source_notes.assessment: Automatic captions and live reading can alter words; transcribe from the printed Comics Journal source before quotation.

source_notes.claim: This is Choe's most famous comics sequence.
source_notes.assessment: It is the hosts' critical/fame judgment, useful for curation but not an objective ranking.

source_notes.claim: The damaged line references the documentary Dirty Hands.
source_notes.assessment: Context strongly suggests the title, but audio and the visible page should be checked before clean promotion.

source_notes.claim: The first-girlfriend and Yumi sequences identify real private people and literal events.
source_notes.assessment: Treat them as comic characters and autobiographical framing; do not identity-resolve from relationship clues.

source_notes.claim: Choe literally attempted suicide and entered a hotel as depicted.
source_notes.assessment: These are plot events in the hosts' reading; do not add them to a biographical timeline without primary corroboration.

source_notes.claim: Choe received the March 1999 Xeric Grant and the named cartoonists were in the stated cycle.
source_notes.assessment: Verify cycle, work titles and recipient list against Xeric Foundation records; one spoken name/title remains badly damaged.

source_notes.claim: The episode made Slow Jams prices rise.
source_notes.assessment: The Kayfabe effect is channel banter and a scarcity pitch, not a controlled appraisal or current market record.
